28.1 i ntroduction
Simple linear regression is restricted in several ways. Primarily, simple linear regression
allows for only one predictor variable. Additionally, this predictor variable must be a quanti-
tative variable. Finally, the response must be a linear function of the predictors. Using mul-
tiple linear regression, discussed in this chapter, we will describe techniques to overcome the
restrictions of simple linear regression.
28.2 s ample s tudy
Let’s continue with our study of Winning Database Configurations: An IBM Informix
Database Survey by Marty Lurie of the IBM Software Group, available at http://www.ibm
.com/developerworks/db2/zones/informix/library/techarticle/lurie/0201lurie.html, by
answering the following questions:
n How is the data stored? What is actually stored the most? Why?
n Why would you expect OLTP databases to have significantly more tables than
decision support databases?
n What was the big surprise in the physical design for Informix?
n What action was taken to avoid being I/O bound?
n What is meant by “fragment elimination”?
n Develop a multiple linear regression analysis for this study using the normalization,
indexing, partitioning, and additional tuning parameters as the predictor variates and
the number of CPUs as the predicted variable.

It should be noted that the Artificial Neural Network (ANN) methodology uses a weighted
sum of input variables to generate a set of output variables similar to the Kelley-Salisbury
method. But what is the relationship between ANNs and multiple linear regression? The
interested reader should study the following sidebar.
c H apter 28 n Introduct I on to Mu L t I p L e L I near r egre SSI on n n n 345
Artificial Neural Networks and Multiple Linear Regression Models
A neural network is essentially a way of simulating a human brain’s activity. The brain is
composed of billions of units referred to as neurons. Each neuron is connected to other
neurons and communicates with them through electrochemical signals. These signals
are captured by synapses, or end branches to the neuron’s cell, called dendrites. Neu-
rons sum up the inputs from the synapses, the inputs, and output a signal on a tail, to the
neuron, referred to as an axon. Artificial neurons are simply an electronic simulation of
biological neurons.
Each artificial neuron acts similar to the Kelley-Salisbury algorithm for a multiple linear
regression equation. When input signals are triggered to the artificial neuron, then the
sum of the weighted input values is submitted to the artificial neuron and an output sig-
nal is activated if it is greater than a threshold value.
In order to link many neurons together, one can start with an initial design of neurons
which are organized into layers. These layers feed their output forward to the next layer
until linking to the final output from the neural network. Input is sent to each neuron in
the innermost layer, actually a hidden layer, and then each hidden layer’s neuron output
is sent to every neuron in the next layer. Such a neural network, referred to as a feed
forward network can have any number of hidden layers.
Neural networks have to be trained. As with the Kelley-Salisbury algorithm for multiple
linear regression, one way of training a neural network is with randomly assigned input
weights. Then a series of inputs, representative of the final desired outputs, are fed into
the artificial neural network. For each configuration of inputs one checks the output

chunks.title: researchmethodsforinformationsystems
chunks.heading: ON DVD
chunks.content:
and adjust the weights accordingly until the network successively recognizes the desired
result. The approach overview in this discussion is referred to as supervised learning.
The data fed into the artificial neural network during training is the training set.
It should be noted that the Kelley-Salisbury algorithm for multiple linear regression
employs only one output, whereas even the simplest neural network, a perception, can
have one or more outputs. Each output has a separate bias and set of weights. Actually,
a perception with a linear activation function is a linear regression model and a percep-
tion with a logistic function is a logistic regression model. In fact, to be more explicit, a
perception with a threshold activation function is a linear discriminant function. With
multiple outputs, the threshold perception is a multiple discriminant function.
Another major difference between artificial neural networks and multiple linear regres-
sion is the number of coefficients per input. Regression coefficients are determined
by the method of least squared error, an optimization technique, whereas, neural nets
employ the method of gradient descent, which allows for multiple coefficients per input.

28.4 t he r elative i mportance of p redictors
Having found the multiple linear regression equation, we would like to evaluate the relative
importance of the independent variables; in other words, which predictors have a large influ-
ence on the dependent variable, and which are less important?
A straightforward and intuitive technique for such evaluations uses the multiple coefficient of
determination R
2
. To discover the importance of one or a group of predictors, the value of R
2
is calculated for the prediction model (called the full model), which includes all the predictor
variables. Then a second model is constructed (the reduced model) from which the predictor
or predictors of interest are excluded, and the value of R
2
for the reduced model is found.

In the method of gradient descent, the gradient vector of the error surface is calculated.
Such vectors are directed along the steepest descent from the current point, therefore,
movement in the current direction will decrease the error. A sequence of these move-
ments will result in a local minimum decrease in error.
This discussion makes it apparent that researchers in information systems need to
undertake a study of artificial neural networks. Multiple linear regression models are
well equipped for linear modeling using optimization strategies. But neural networks are
capable of modeling in nonlinear instances. The interested reader should view Neural
Networks: Tutorial Slides by Andrew Moore found at http://www.autonlab.org/tutorials/
neural.html and Neural Networks and Statistical Models by Warren Sarle, SAS Institute
Inc. that was presented at the Proceedings of the Nineteenth Annual SAS Users Group
International Conference in April, 1994.

greater than, rather than less than, a = 5%.
